# Introduction

## Context and Scientific Motivation

\textbf{Spatial Interpolation:}
A fundamental technique in environmental sciences to estimate continuous variables at unsampled locations based \textbf{exclusively on spatial coordinates}.

\vspace{1em}

\textbf{Evolution of the Paradigm:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Traditional:} \geobadge{} and \detbadge{} — foundations in spatial continuity
  \item \textbf{Modern:} \mlbadge{} — capable of modeling complex, non-linear spatial surfaces
\end{itemize}

\vspace{1em}

## Research Question

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=ensaiblue!10, colframe=ensaiblue, arc=5pt, boxrule=1pt]
\centering
\textbf{Which algorithm is most effective for predicting spatial values\\using coordinates as the only covariates?}
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.6em}

The "optimal" model is defined through \textbf{two critical dimensions}:

\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Predictive Precision}: Ability to minimize error across diverse spatial geometries
  \item \textbf{Scalability}: Computational efficiency transitioning from sparse to large-scale, high-density data
\end{enumerate}

## Core Hypothesis

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=accentgold!18, colframe=accentgold!85, arc=5pt, boxrule=1.2pt]
\centering
\textbf{Coordinate Rotation integrated into ensemble methods\\can effectively replace or outperform traditional deterministic algorithms}
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.8em}

\textbf{Motivation:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Standard tree-based models struggle with axis-aligned splits in spatial contexts
  \item Transforming feature space can unlock significantly higher performance
  \item Goal: Rigorously test capabilities and limitations of coordinate rotation in spatial modeling
\end{itemize}

## Deterministic Methods

\begin{columns}[T]

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{detblue}{Inverse Distance Weighting}}
    \vspace{0.15cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=detblue, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=L]
    {\small Prediction as a distance-weighted average:}
    \[
    \hat{z}(s_0) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i(s_0)\, z(s_i)}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i(s_0)}
    \]
    {\small with weights:}
    \[
    w_i(s_0) = \frac{1}{d(s_0, s_i)^p}
    \]
    {\footnotesize $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ = Euclidean distance \quad $p > 0$ = decay exponent}
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{detblue}{K-Nearest Neighbors}}
    \vspace{0.15cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=detblue, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=L]
    {\small Prediction as average of the $k$ closest observations:}
    \[
    \hat{z}(s_0) = \frac{1}{k} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{N}_k(s_0)} z(s_i)
    \]
    {\footnotesize $\mathcal{N}_k(s_0)$ = set of $k$ nearest neighbors of $s_0$}
    \vspace{0.2cm}

    {\small Optionally using distance-based weights.}
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

\end{columns}

\vspace{0.2cm}
\centering
{\footnotesize \textcolor{gray}{Both methods rely \textbf{purely on geometric principles} — no training phase, no statistical model.}}

## Deterministic $\neq$ Assumption-Free

\begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=gray, colback=gray!8, arc=4pt, boxrule=1pt]
\centering
{\small \textit{``Deterministic does not mean assumption-free!''}}
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.1cm}

\begin{columns}[T]

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{detblue}{IDW — the exponent $p$}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=detblue, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt]
    {\footnotesize
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] Large $p$ $\Rightarrow$ only nearest points matter
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] Small $p$ $\Rightarrow$ distant points still contribute
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] Controls how fast spatial influence \textbf{decays with distance}
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{detblue}{K-NN — the parameter $k$}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=detblue, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt]
    {\footnotesize
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] Small $k$ $\Rightarrow$ highly local, noisy predictions
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] Large $k$ $\Rightarrow$ strong smoothing effect
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] Controls the \textbf{spatial bandwidth} of the interpolation
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

\end{columns}

\vspace{0.1cm}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=detblue, colback=detblue!8, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt]
\centering
{\small Both methods embed \textbf{implicit assumptions about the underlying spatial process through the choice of hyperparameters}}
\end{tcolorbox}

## Deterministic Methods: Strengths \& Limitations

\begin{columns}[T]

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{detblue}{Strengths}}
    \vspace{0.1cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=detblue, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=G]
    {\small
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Near-instant training} — no fitting phase required
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Highly scalable} — competitive even on very large datasets
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Fully interpretable} — prediction mechanism is transparent
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Strong baseline} — any ML gain must be justified against them
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{detblue}{Limitations}}
    \vspace{0.1cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=detblue, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=G]
    {\small
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{No learning mechanism} — fixed rules, cannot adapt to data
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Monotonic distance assumption} — influence always decays smoothly
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Miss complex spatial structures} — cannot capture anisotropy
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Fragile to noise} — error degrades significantly under noisy conditions
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

\end{columns}

## Kriging: A Geostatistical Approach

\begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=geoviolet!8, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt]
\centering
{\small Kriging goes beyond fixed rules — it models the \textbf{spatial structure} of the data itself, learning how observations relate to each other across space.}
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.15cm}

\begin{columns}[T]

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{geoviolet}{Idea}}
    \vspace{0.1cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=F]
    {\footnotesize
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] Nearby observations tend to be similar
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] \textit{How similar?} — captured by the \textbf{variogram}
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] Variogram describes how similarity \textbf{changes with distance}
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] Weights derived by \textbf{minimizing prediction error variance}
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{geoviolet}{Types of Kriging}}
    \vspace{0.1cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=F]
    {\footnotesize
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Simple Kriging} — known constant mean
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Universal Kriging} — polynomial drift
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Ordinary Kriging} — unknown constant mean
    \end{itemize}
    \vspace{0.15cm}
    \centering
    $\Rightarrow$ This benchmark focuses on \textbf{Ordinary Kriging}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

\end{columns}

## Ordinary Kriging: The BLUP

\begin{columns}[T]

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{geoviolet}{The Predictor}}
    \vspace{0.1cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=E]
    {\footnotesize Linear combination of observed values:}
    \[
    \hat{Z}(s_0) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i\, Z(s_i)
    \]
    {\footnotesize subject to unbiasedness constraint:}
    \[
    \sum_{i=1}^{n} \lambda_i = 1
    \]
    {\footnotesize Weights $\lambda_i$ minimize $\text{Var}(\hat{Z}(s_0) - Z(s_0))$}
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{geoviolet}{Theoretical Advantages}}
    \vspace{0.1cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=E]
    {\footnotesize
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{BLUP} — Best Linear Unbiased Predictor under its \textbf{assumptions}
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Exact interpolation} at observed locations
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Smooth surfaces} — no abrupt artifacts
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Uncertainty estimates} — natural confidence intervals
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

\end{columns}

\vspace{0.15cm}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=geoviolet!8, arc=4pt, boxrule=1pt]
\centering
{\small \textit{Theoretically optimal — but optimality holds only under its \textbf{assumptions}.}}
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.4cm}

## Kriging: Statistical Assumptions

\begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=geoviolet!8, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt]
\centering
{\small Kriging's guarantees rely on assumptions \textbf{often violated in real-world scenarios}.}
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.1cm}

\begin{columns}[T]

  \begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{geoviolet}{Stationarity}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=I]
    {\footnotesize
    Assumes a \textbf{constant mean} over the entire spatial domain and a variogram that depends only on the distance between points, not on their absolute location.
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{geoviolet}{Isotropy}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=I]
    {\footnotesize
    Assumes spatial correlation depends \textbf{only on distance}, not on direction. Any directional effect in the data causes the variogram model to become misspecified.
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{geoviolet}{Gaussianity}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=I]
    {\footnotesize
    Implicitly assumes \textbf{Gaussian distributed} data. Skewed or heavy-tailed variables require prior transformations, adding subjectivity to the modeling pipeline.
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

\end{columns}

\vspace{0.1cm}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=geoviolet!8, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt]
\centering
{\small When assumptions fail $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{biased predictions} and \textbf{distorted uncertainty estimates}}
\end{tcolorbox}

## Kriging: Computational Limitations

\begin{columns}[T]

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{geoviolet}{Cubic Complexity}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=J]
    {\footnotesize
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] Requires inversion of an $n \times n$ covariance matrix
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] Complexity: $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Prohibitively slow} for datasets larger than $\sim$10,000 points
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] Excluded from large-scale tests in this benchmark
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{geoviolet}{Variogram Estimation}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=J]
    {\footnotesize
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] Must select a theoretical model (spherical, exponential, Gaussian\ldots) and fit its parameters: \textbf{nugget}, \textbf{sill}, and \textbf{range}
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] Fitting is \textbf{partly subjective}, demands experience and is sensitive to outliers
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] Prediction quality depends \textbf{directly} on variogram specification — a poor fit leads to unreliable estimates
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

\end{columns}

\vspace{0.15cm}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=geoviolet!8, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt]
\centering
{\small \textbf{Theoretically optimal under its assumptions — but impractical at scale.}}
\end{tcolorbox}

## Machine Learning: A New Paradigm

\begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=treeOrange, colback=treeOrange!8, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt]
\centering
{\small ML algorithms \textbf{learn predictive relationships directly from the data} — no fixed rules, no explicit stochastic models.}
\end{tcolorbox}

\vspace{0.1cm}

\begin{columns}[T]

  \begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{detblue}{Deterministic}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=detblue, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=K]
    {\footnotesize
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] Fixed mathematical rules
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] No training phase
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] Implicit assumptions via hyperparameters
      \item[\textcolor{detblue}{$\bullet$}] Fragile to noise
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{geoviolet}{Geostatistical}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=geoviolet, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=K]
    {\footnotesize
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] Explicit stochastic model
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] Strong assumptions required
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] Optimal under assumptions
      \item[\textcolor{geoviolet}{$\bullet$}] Complexity $\mathcal{O}(n^3)$
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{advRed}{Machine Learning}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=advRed, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=K]
    {\footnotesize
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{advRed}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Data-driven}
      \item[\textcolor{advRed}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{No strong assumptions}
      \item[\textcolor{advRed}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Highly scalable}
      \item[\textcolor{advRed}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Extensible} to additional covariates
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

\end{columns}

## ML Methods: Two Families

\begin{columns}[T]

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{treeOrange}{Tree-Based Ensemble Methods}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=treeOrange, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=H]
    {\footnotesize
    Combine many \textbf{decision trees} — predictions aggregated across the ensemble.
    \vspace{0.1cm}

    \textit{In this benchmark:}
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{treeOrange}{$\bullet$}] Random Forest
      \item[\textcolor{treeOrange}{$\bullet$}] XGBoost
      \item[\textcolor{treeOrange}{$\bullet$}] MI-GBT
      \item[\textcolor{advRed}{$\bullet$}] GeoSpatial RF
      \item[\textcolor{advRed}{$\bullet$}] Oblique RF
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{gamGreen}{Generalized Additive Models}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=gamGreen, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=H]
    {\footnotesize
    Target modeled as a \textbf{sum of smooth functions} of the inputs:
    \[
    g(\mu) = \alpha + f_1(x_1) + \cdots + f_p(x_p)
    \]
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{gamGreen}{$\bullet$}] More \textbf{interpretable} than ensemble methods
      \item[\textcolor{gamGreen}{$\bullet$}] Captures \textbf{nonlinear spatial trends}
      \item[\textcolor{gamGreen}{$\bullet$}] Limited on \textbf{complex interactions}
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

\end{columns}

## Tree-Based Methods: Bagging vs Boosting

\begin{columns}[T]

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{treeOrange}{Random Forest — Bagging}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=treeOrange, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=B]
    {\footnotesize
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{treeOrange}{$\bullet$}] Trees trained \textbf{in parallel} on bootstrap samples
      \item[\textcolor{treeOrange}{$\bullet$}] Random subset of features at each split
      \item[\textcolor{treeOrange}{$\bullet$}] Predictions \textbf{averaged} across all trees
      \item[\textcolor{treeOrange}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Reduced variance}, robust, stable
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{treeOrange}{Gradient Boosting — XGBoost, MI-GBT}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=treeOrange, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=B]
    {\footnotesize
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{treeOrange}{$\bullet$}] Trees built \textbf{sequentially} — each corrects residuals of the previous
      \item[\textcolor{treeOrange}{$\bullet$}] Iterative refinement $\Rightarrow$ \textbf{higher accuracy}
      \item[\textcolor{treeOrange}{$\bullet$}] Higher risk of \textbf{overfitting} if not regularized
      \item[\textcolor{treeOrange}{$\bullet$}] More sensitive to \textbf{hyperparameter tuning}
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

\end{columns}

\vspace{0.1cm}

\begin{center}
\begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=treeOrange, colback=treeOrange!8, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, width=0.75\textwidth]
\centering
{\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{lcc}
 & \textbf{Random Forest} & \textbf{Gradient Boosting} \\[2pt]
\textit{Training} & Parallel & Sequential \\
\textit{Accuracy} & Good & Higher \\
\textit{Overfitting risk} & Low & Moderate \\
\textit{Tuning sensitivity} & Low & High \\
\end{tabular}
}
\end{tcolorbox}
\end{center}

## Tree-Based Methods on Spatial Data: The Challenges

\begin{columns}[T]

  \begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{treeOrange}{Spatial Autocorrelation}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=treeOrange, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=C]
    {\footnotesize
    Nearby observations tend to have \textbf{similar values}. Standard trees do not account for this dependence structure and may \textbf{overfit local noise}.
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{treeOrange}{Anisotropy}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=treeOrange, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=C]
    {\footnotesize
    Spatial dependence may vary \textbf{with direction}, not just distance. Axis-aligned splits produce only \textbf{N-S or E-W} boundaries — oblique patterns require many splits to approximate.
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.31\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{treeOrange}{Large-Scale Trends}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=treeOrange, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=C]
    {\footnotesize
    Smooth gradients spanning the entire domain — elevation, temperature, housing prices. Trees approximate these with \textbf{stepwise partitions}, leading to deep trees and potential overfitting.
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

\end{columns}

\vspace{0.1cm}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=treeOrange, colback=treeOrange!8, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt]
\centering
{\small Standard tree-based models \textbf{are not specifically designed} for geospatial data — adaptation is required to unlock their full potential.}
\end{tcolorbox}

## Adapting Tree-Based Methods to Spatial Data

\vspace{0.1cm}

\begin{columns}[T]

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{stratTeal}{Strategy 1 — Modify the Algorithm}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=stratTeal, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=D]
    {\footnotesize
    \textbf{GeoSpatial RF:}
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{stratTeal}{$\bullet$}] Incorporates \textbf{spatial information} into ensemble construction
    \end{itemize}
    \textbf{Oblique RF:}
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{stratTeal}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Oblique splits} not constrained to axes
      \item[\textcolor{stratTeal}{$\bullet$}] Naturally captures \textbf{spatial gradients}
    \end{itemize}
    \textbf{Drawback:} computationally demanding
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \centering
    \textbf{\textcolor{stratTeal}{Strategy 2 — Coordinate Rotation}}
    \vspace{0.05cm}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=stratTeal, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=D]
    {\footnotesize
    A novel preprocessing strategy that \textbf{augments the feature space} with rotated versions of the original spatial coordinates.

    \vspace{0.1cm}
    The hypothesis: this simple transformation could allow standard tree-based models to \textbf{overcome their geometric limitations} — without sacrificing scalability.

    \vspace{0.1cm}
    \textbf{Applied to:} RF, XGBoost, MI-GBT, GAM
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

\end{columns}

\vspace{0.15cm}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=stratTeal, colback=stratTeal!8, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt]
\centering
{\small \textbf{The true goal of this benchmark:} does Coordinate Rotation improve predictive accuracy — and is the gain worth the computational cost?}
\end{tcolorbox}

# Coordinate Rotation

## The Problem: Axis-Aligned Splits

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.52\textwidth}

\textbf{Geometric Constraint:}
Standard tree-based methods rely \textbf{exclusively on axis-aligned splits} during construction.

\vspace{0.6em}

\textbf{In spatial context:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Splits constrained to \textbf{North-South} or \textbf{East-West} orientations
  \item Diagonal patterns approximated via \textbf{staircase accumulation}
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.6em}

\textbf{Impact:}
Many recursive splits needed for oblique boundaries

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.44\textwidth}

\centering
\begin{tikzpicture}[scale=0.85]
  \draw[->] (0,0) -- (4.5,0) node[right] {East};
  \draw[->] (0,0) -- (0,4.5) node[above] {North};

  \draw[detcol, ultra thick] (0,1.5) -- (1.5,1.5) -- (1.5,2.5) -- (2.5,2.5) -- (2.5,3.5) -- (4,3.5);
  \node[mlcol] at (2.8,3.3) {\small\textbf{True pattern}};
  \node[detcol] at (3.2,0.9) {\small\textbf{Tree approximation}};
\end{tikzpicture}

\end{column}
\end{columns}


## Two Strategies to Overcome Limitations

\begin{columns}[T]

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=stratTeal, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=M]
    {\footnotesize
    \textbf{Oblique Decision Trees}
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{stratTeal}{$\bullet$}] Directly learn \textbf{oblique splits}
      \item[\textcolor{stratTeal}{$\bullet$}] Linear combinations at each node
      \item[\textcolor{stratTeal}{$\bullet$}] Flexible geometry
      \item[\textcolor{stratTeal}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Computationally demanding}
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

  \begin{column}{0.48\textwidth}
    \begin{tcolorbox}[colframe=stratTeal, colback=white, arc=4pt, boxrule=1.2pt, equal height group=M]
    {\footnotesize
    \textbf{Coordinate Rotation (CR)}
    \begin{itemize}
      \item[\textcolor{stratTeal}{$\bullet$}] Augment feature space with \textbf{rotated coordinates}
      \item[\textcolor{stratTeal}{$\bullet$}] Standard axis-aligned algorithm
      \item[\textcolor{stratTeal}{$\bullet$}] Effective oblique learning
      \item[\textcolor{stratTeal}{$\bullet$}] \textbf{Low computational overhead}
    \end{itemize}
    }
    \end{tcolorbox}
  \end{column}

\end{columns}


## Rotation Method: Feature Augmentation

\textbf{Transformation Procedure:}
Rotations applied around the \textbf{centroid} $(\bar{x}, \bar{y})$ for $k$ axes

\vspace{0.5em}

\begin{enumerate}
  \item Compute spatial centroid:
  $$\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i, \quad \bar{y} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n y_i$$

  \item Generate rotation angles: $\theta_j = \frac{360^\circ \cdot j}{k}$ \quad for $j = 0, 1, \ldots, k-1$

  \item For each angle $\theta_j$, transform all points:
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{0.1em}

\formulabox{ensaiblue}{
$$x'_{ij} = \bar{x} + (x_i - \bar{x})\cos\theta_j - (y_i - \bar{y})\sin\theta_j$$
$$y'_{ij} = \bar{y} + (x_i - \bar{x})\sin\theta_j + (y_i - \bar{y})\cos\theta_j$$
}


## Geometric Interpretation

\begin{columns}
\begin{column}{0.50\textwidth}

\textbf{Change of Reference System:}
Each rotation defines a new coordinate system oriented at angle $\theta_j$ w.r.t. the original.

\vspace{0.6em}

\textbf{Key Property:}
Spatial patterns appearing \textbf{oblique} in original coordinates may become \textbf{axis-aligned} in a rotated system.

\vspace{0.6em}

\textbf{Augmented Feature Space:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item Original: $(x, y)$
  \item After CR: $(x, y, x'_1, y'_1, \ldots, x'_{k-1}, y'_{k-1})$
  \item Trees auto-select best orientation per split
\end{itemize}

\end{column}
\begin{column}{0.46\textwidth}

\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{coordinaterotation_converted.png}

\vspace{0.5em}

\begin{tcolorbox}[colback=ensaiblue!8, colframe=ensaiblue!70, arc=4pt]
\small\centering
\textbf{Computational Efficiency:} $O(nk)$ preprocessing
\end{tcolorbox}

\end{column}
\end{columns}

## Validation Strategy and Metrics

\textbf{Performance Metrics:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{$R^2$}: Scale-invariant overall fit \quad $\bullet$ \quad \textbf{RMSE}: Penalizes large errors
  \item \textbf{MAE}: Robust to outliers \quad $\bullet$ \quad \textbf{Training Time}: Practical scalability
\end{itemize}

\vspace{0.6em}

\textbf{Two-Phase Selection Strategy:}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item Benchmark all algorithms on small datasets ($N \approx 5$k)
  \item Preselect efficient candidates for larger datasets
\end{enumerate}

\vspace{0.6em}

\textbf{Benchmark Procedure:}
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Validation:} Randomized Search with K-Fold Cross-Validation
  \item \textbf{Adaptive tuning:} Small datasets (20 iter, 5-fold, 10min timeout) $\rightarrow$ Large datasets (5 iter, 3-fold)
  \item \textbf{CR Implementation:} 23 rotation angles \quad $\bullet$ \quad \textbf{Environment:} Python 3.13, SSPCloud
  \item \textbf{Reproducibility:} Fixed seeds (42 for models, 20170519 for synthetic data)
\end{itemize}

# Results

```{python}
#| echo: false

# ============================================================================
# 0. GLOBAL CONFIGURATION & DATA LOADING
# ============================================================================
import json
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd
from pathlib import Path
from math import pi

sns.set_style("white")
plt.rcParams['figure.dpi'] = 300
plt.rcParams['font.size'] = 11

# --- Loading Data ---
results = []
def load_json_results(filename):
    path = Path(filename)
    if path.exists():
        with open(path, 'r') as f:
            data = json.load(f)
            if isinstance(data, list): return data
            if isinstance(data, dict) and 'results' in data: return data['results']
    return []

# Attempt to load files
results.extend(load_json_results('results/results_small.json'))
results.extend(load_json_results('results/results_large_noisy.json'))

# Fallback if files are missing (avoids compilation errors)
if not results and Path('example.json').exists():
    with open('example.json', 'r') as f:
        results = json.load(f)['results']

df = pd.DataFrame(results)
if 'training_time' in df.columns:
    df['time_train'] = df['training_time'].fillna(df.get('time_train', 0))

# --- Definitions ---
deterministic_models = ['knn_3', 'idw_p3']
geostatistical_models = ['kriging']
tree_models = ['random_forest', 'random_forest_cr', 'xgboost', 'xgboost_cr', 'mixgboost', 'mixgboost_cr']
advanced_tree_models = ['oblique_rf', 'geoRF']
gam_models = ['gam', 'gam_cr']

model_names = {
    'random_forest': 'RF', 'random_forest_cr': 'RF-CR',
    'xgboost': 'XGB', 'xgboost_cr': 'XGB-CR',
    'mixgboost': 'MiGBT', 'mixgboost_cr': 'MiGBT-CR',
    'oblique_rf': 'Oblique RF', 'geoRF': 'GeoRF',
    'knn_3': 'KNN', 'idw_p3': 'IDW',
    'kriging': 'Kriging', 'gam': 'GAM', 'gam_cr': 'GAM-CR'
}

dataset_names = {
    'rgealti_48': 'Real Grid Small',
    'rgealti': 'Real Grid Large',
    'bdalti_48': 'Real No-Grid Small',
    'bdalti': 'Real No-Grid Large',
    'S-G-Sm': 'Synth Grid Small',
    'S-G-Lg': 'Synth Grid Large',
    'S-NG-Sm': 'Synth No-Grid Small',
    'S-NG-Lg': 'Synth No-Grid Large',
    'S-G-Lg-N': 'Synth Grid Large (Noisy)',
    'S-NG-Lg-N': 'Synth No-Grid Large (Noisy)',
    'cal_housing': 'Housing (Real Noisy)'
}

color_deterministic = '#2E86AB'
color_geostat = '#A23B72'
color_tree = '#F18F01'
color_advanced_tree = '#C73E1D'
color_gam = '#6A994E'

def get_model_color(model):
    if model in deterministic_models: return color_deterministic
    if model in geostatistical_models: return color_geostat
    if model in tree_models: return color_tree
    if model in advanced_tree_models: return color_advanced_tree
    if model in gam_models: return color_gam
    return '#888888'
```

```{python}
#| echo: false

from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
import matplotlib.ticker as ticker

def plot_small_datasets_landscape():
    small_ds = ['rgealti_48', 'bdalti_48', 'S-G-Sm', 'S-NG-Sm']
    ds_shapes = {'rgealti_48': 'o', 'bdalti_48': 's', 'S-G-Sm': '^', 'S-NG-Sm': 'D'}

    plot_data = []
    for m_key in model_names.keys():
        for ds in small_ds:
            res = next((r for r in results if r['model'] == m_key and r['dataset'] == ds), None)
            if res:
                val_rmse = res.get('rmse', np.sqrt(res.get('mse', 0)))
                plot_data.append({
                    'ModelKey': m_key,
                    'Dataset': dataset_names.get(ds, ds),
                    'Time': res.get('training_time', 0.001),
                    'RMSE': val_rmse,
                    'Color': get_model_color(m_key),
                    'Shape': ds_shapes[ds]
                })

    df = pd.DataFrame(plot_data)

    # On utilise un format plus large (12) et moins haut (4.5) pour le 16:9 de Beamer
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(12, 4.5))

    for _, row in df.iterrows():
        ax.scatter(row['Time'], row['RMSE'],
                   c=row['Color'], marker=row['Shape'],
                   s=80, alpha=0.7, edgecolors='black', linewidth=0.6, zorder=3)

    ax.set_xscale('log')

    # Formatage propre de l'axe X (évite les 10^-3, etc.)
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(ticker.ScalarFormatter())
    ax.set_xlabel('Training Time (seconds) - Log Scale', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_ylabel('RMSE', fontsize=10, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_title('Efficiency vs. Accuracy Trade-off (Small Datasets)', fontweight='bold', pad=15)

    ax.grid(True, which="both", linestyle='--', alpha=0.2, zorder=0)

    # --- LEGENDES (Positionnées à l'extérieur pour libérer l'espace) ---
    legend_elements_color = [
        Line2D([0], [0], marker='o', color='w', markerfacecolor=color_deterministic, markersize=9, label='Deterministic'),
        Line2D([0], [0], marker='o', color='w', markerfacecolor=color_tree, markersize=9, label='Tree Ensemble'),
        Line2D([0], [0], marker='o', color='w', markerfacecolor=color_advanced_tree, markersize=9, label='Advanced Tree'),
        Line2D([0], [0], marker='o', color='w', markerfacecolor=color_geostat, markersize=9, label='Geostatistical'),
        Line2D([0], [0], marker='o', color='w', markerfacecolor=color_gam, markersize=9, label='GAM'),
    ]

    leg1 = ax.legend(handles=legend_elements_color, title="Algorithm Family",
                     bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 1), loc='upper left', borderaxespad=0., fontsize=9)
    ax.add_artist(leg1)

    legend_elements_shape = [
        Line2D([0], [0], marker=ds_shapes[ds], color='w', markerfacecolor='gray',
               markeredgecolor='black', markersize=7, label=dataset_names.get(ds, ds))
        for ds in small_ds
    ]

    ax.legend(handles=legend_elements_shape, title="Dataset Source",
              bbox_to_anchor=(1.02, 0.35), loc='upper left', borderaxespad=0., fontsize=9)

    # CRUCIAL : On force la marge à droite pour laisser de la place aux légendes
    # et en bas pour que l'axe X ne soit pas coupé
    plt.subplots_adjust(right=0.72, bottom=0.22, top=0.88)

    sns.despine()
    plt.show()

plot_small_datasets_landscape()
```

## Scalability: Augmentation Factor

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

# ==========================================
# Average Large Time / Average Small Time
# ==========================================
small_datasets = ['S-G-Sm', 'S-NG-Sm', 'rgealti_48', 'bdalti_48']
large_datasets = ['S-G-Lg', 'S-NG-Lg', 'rgealti', 'bdalti']

df_small = df[df['dataset'].isin(small_datasets)].copy()
df_large = df[df['dataset'].isin(large_datasets)].copy()

if not df_small.empty and not df_large.empty:
    avg_small = df_small.groupby('model')['time_train'].mean()
    avg_large = df_large.groupby('model')['time_train'].mean()

    aug_df = pd.DataFrame({'small': avg_small, 'large': avg_large}).dropna()
    aug_df['Factor'] = aug_df['large'] / aug_df['small']
    aug_df = aug_df.sort_values('Factor')

    aug_df['Display'] = [model_names.get(x, x) for x in aug_df.index]
    colors = [get_model_color(x) for x in aug_df.index]

    # Adjusted figsize to be wider and shorter (11, 4.5)
    plt.figure(figsize=(11, 4.5))
    ax = sns.barplot(x='Display', y='Factor', data=aug_df, palette=colors)

    plt.axhline(1, color='#333333', linestyle='--', linewidth=1, alpha=0.5)
    plt.title('Scalability: Training Time Augmentation Factor\n(Average Large Time / Average Small Time)', fontweight='bold')
    plt.ylabel('Multiplier (x times slower)')
    plt.xlabel('')
    plt.xticks(rotation=45, ha='right')

    for i, v in enumerate(aug_df['Factor']):
        ax.text(i, v + (v * 0.05), f"{v:.1f}x", ha='center', va='bottom', fontweight='bold', fontsize=10)

    sns.despine()
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

## Robustness Ranking

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

# ==========================================
# Bump Chart (Constant Distance)
# ==========================================
noise_map = {
    'S-NG-Lg': 'Clean\n(σ=0)', 'S-NG-Lg-N1': 'Low Noise\n(σ=0.5)',
    'S-NG-Lg-N2': 'Med Noise\n(σ=1.0)', 'S-NG-Lg-N3': 'High Noise\n(σ=2.0)'
}
noise_order = list(noise_map.keys())
subset = df[df['dataset'].isin(noise_order)].copy()

if not subset.empty:
    pivot = subset.pivot(index='model', columns='dataset', values='rmse')[noise_order]
    ranks = pivot.rank(axis=0, method='first', ascending=True)
    diffs = -ranks.diff(axis=1)

    # Adjusted figsize (11, 5.5) - Needs height for ranking, but controlled
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5.5))
    coords = {i: {} for i in range(len(noise_order))}

    for col_idx, col_key in enumerate(noise_order):
        current_ranks = ranks[col_key].sort_values()
        for model, rank in current_ranks.items():
            rmse = pivot.loc[model, col_key]
            y_pos = rank
            coords[col_idx][model] = y_pos

            name = model_names.get(model, model)
            color = get_model_color(model)

            change_text, c_color = "", "gray"
            if col_idx > 0:
                chg = diffs.loc[model, col_key]
                if chg > 0: change_text, c_color = f"▲", "#27ae60"
                elif chg < 0: change_text, c_color = f"▼", "#c0392b"
                else: change_text, c_color = "=", "#bdc3c7"

            ax.text(col_idx - 0.1, y_pos, f"{int(rank)}", ha='right', va='center',
                    fontsize=10, fontweight='bold', color='#95a5a6')

            box_props = dict(facecolor='white', edgecolor='none', alpha=0.8, pad=0.3)
            ax.text(col_idx, y_pos, f"{name}", ha='center', va='center',
                    fontsize=9, fontweight='bold', color=color, bbox=box_props)

            if change_text:
                ax.text(col_idx + 0.15, y_pos, change_text, ha='left', va='center',
                        fontsize=8, fontweight='bold', color=c_color)

    for model in pivot.index:
        color = get_model_color(model)
        lw = 2.5 if model in ['knn_3', 'idw_p3', 'random_forest_cr'] else 1
        alpha = 0.5 if model in ['knn_3', 'idw_p3'] else 0.2
        ys = [coords[i].get(model) for i in range(len(noise_order))]
        if None not in ys:
            ax.plot(range(len(noise_order)), ys, color=color, alpha=alpha, linewidth=lw, zorder=0)

    ax.set_ylim(len(pivot)+0.5, 0.5)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.3, len(noise_order) - 0.7)

    ax.xaxis.tick_top()
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(noise_order)))
    ax.set_xticklabels([noise_map[k] for k in noise_order], fontsize=11, fontweight='bold')
    ax.set_yticks([])
    sns.despine(left=True, bottom=True, right=True, top=True)

    for x in range(len(noise_order) - 1):
        ax.axvline(x + 0.5, color='#ecf0f1', linestyle='-', linewidth=2)

    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()
```

## Cost vs. Benefit : Coordinates Rotation

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center

# ==========================================
# Radar Charts
# ==========================================
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from math import pi
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

models_to_plot = [
    ('random_forest', 'random_forest_cr', 'Random Forest'),
    ('xgboost', 'xgboost_cr', 'XGBoost'),
    ('mixgboost', 'mixgboost_cr', 'MiGBT')
]

# Create subplots: 1 Row, 3 Columns
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(14, 5), subplot_kw=dict(polar=True))

# Shared Legend Elements
legend_elements = [
    Line2D([0], [0], color='#2ecc71', lw=2, label='Precision Gain (Factor)'),
    Line2D([0], [0], color='#e74c3c', lw=2, label='Time Cost (Factor)')
]

for i, (base_model, cr_model, title) in enumerate(models_to_plot):
    ax = axes[i]

    # Get Data
    base_df = df[df['model'] == base_model].set_index('dataset')
    cr_df = df[df['model'] == cr_model].set_index('dataset')
    common = base_df.index.intersection(cr_df.index)
    friendly_ds = [d for d in common if d in dataset_names]

    p_data, t_data, labels = [], [], []

    for ds in friendly_ds:
        b_rmse, b_time = base_df.loc[ds, 'rmse'], base_df.loc[ds, 'time_train']
        c_rmse, c_time = cr_df.loc[ds, 'rmse'], cr_df.loc[ds, 'time_train']

        if c_rmse > 0 and b_time > 0:
            p_factor = b_rmse / c_rmse
            t_factor = c_time / b_time
            if p_factor < 10 and t_factor < 10:
                p_data.append(p_factor)
                t_data.append(t_factor)
                labels.append(dataset_names[ds])

    if len(labels) >= 3:
        # Closing loops
        labels_plot = labels
        angles = [n / float(len(labels_plot)) * 2 * pi for n in range(len(labels_plot))]
        angles += [angles[0]]
        p_data += [p_data[0]]
        t_data += [t_data[0]]

        ax.set_theta_offset(pi / 2)
        ax.set_theta_direction(-1)

        # Labels
        ax.set_xticks(angles[:-1])
        ax.set_xticklabels(labels_plot, size=8, fontweight='bold')
        ax.set_rlabel_position(0)

        # Plots
        ax.plot(angles, t_data, linewidth=2, linestyle='-', color='#e74c3c')
        ax.fill(angles, t_data, color='#e74c3c', alpha=0.3)

        ax.plot(angles, p_data, linewidth=2, linestyle='-', color='#2ecc71')
        ax.fill(angles, p_data, color='#2ecc71', alpha=0.3)

        ax.plot(angles, [1.0]*len(angles), linewidth=1, linestyle='--', color='black', alpha=0.5)

        ax.set_title(title, size=12, weight='bold', pad=15)
        # Fix overlapping labels with padding
        ax.tick_params(pad=10)

# Single Legend at Bottom
fig.legend(handles=legend_elements, loc='lower center',
           bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=2, fontsize=10)

plt.tight_layout()
# Add space for legend
plt.subplots_adjust(bottom=0.2)
plt.show()
```
